newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil on course for 3.0 pct current account gap.
newsitem.headline: Brazil on course for 3.0 pct current account gap.

text.p: Brazil is on course for a year-end current account deficit of three percent of gross domestic product, said Altamir Lopes, head of the Central Bank's economics department.

Lopes said a sharp widening in the gap to 2.89 percent of GDP in October from 2.53 percent in September was due to special factors affecting services: high interest on external debt and low transfers from Brazilians abroad.
"A 3.0 percent deficit for the end of the year is still on because interest payments will return to normal," he told reporters. "Evidently, a lot depends on the trade performance."
The services account in October was pressured by $1.3 billion in Brady bond interest payments, and also a $355 million payment to the Paris Club of creditor nations.
Private sector payments on external debt were also high, Lopes said.
In the January-to-October period, Brazil paid out $8.268 billion in interest, against $7.202 billion in the year-ago period.

Unilateral transfers, composed primarily of money sent back by Brazilian-Japanese and to a lesser extent by Brazilian nationals in the United States, slumped to $2.513 billion in the 10-month period from $3.376 billion a year earlier.

Lopes said that was the result of lower returns on Brazilian instruments, tighter restrictions on so-called CC5 accounts held by foreigners in Brazil and also dollar-yen exchange rates, making dollars more expensive to yen-holders.
"What really pressured the services account was the $1.3 billion Brady payment," he said.
